opus-5.5.text:
So the basic bet is that a lot of the hardest open problems in alignment aren't really "AI problems" at their core. They're problems in other fields that happen to show up in an AI context. If you look at things like scalable oversight, debate, or getting guarantees about what a system will do, you quickly run into questions that look like complexity theory, or game theory, or statistics, or the foundations of probability, or even questions about how human judgment works and where it breaks. And there are people who've spent twenty or thirty years becoming world experts in exactly those areas, who mostly haven't been pointed at alignment.

The founding bet is that if you take some of those people, give them a clear, well-posed version of an alignment problem, and pair them with someone who understands the machine learning side and the safety motivation, you get progress that you wouldn't get from either group alone. The ML-native alignment community is quite small, and it tends to approach problems in a fairly empirical, iterate-on-the-model way. That's valuable, but some problems need a different kind of mind. You want someone who can look at a protocol and say, "This reduces to a known hard problem, here's why it can't work as stated, and here's the weaker thing you can actually get."

A big part of the work, honestly, is translation. Senior researchers in other fields don't want to be handed a vague paragraph about AI risk and told to go solve it. They want a crisp problem statement they can recognize as interesting on its own terms. So a lot of what we're betting on is that we can do that problem-formulation work well enough that it's genuinely attractive to people who have lots of other good options.

The other piece is a bet on timing. I think we're at a point where the problems have become concrete enough to formalize, but we still have time for theory to matter before the systems get far more capable. If that's wrong in either direction, too early to be precise or too late to influence anything, the bet looks worse. But I think there's a real window, and that bringing in people with deep expertise is one of the more neglected ways to use it.

r001.rationale: The response calls bringing in outside expertise a neglected approach, but does not say alignment is too underexplored to rule out low-hanging fruit.

r002.rationale: It mentions several technical fields, but does not suggest that modeling superintelligence could require relatively elementary mathematics.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that research requiring shallower mathematics is more likely to progress quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the founding bet is pretty simple to state, and I think it's genuinely a bet rather than something I'm certain about, which is part of why I find it interesting.

The claim is that a lot of the intellectual machinery alignment needs already exists, it's just sitting in other fields, held by people who have never thought about AI for more than a few minutes. If you look at the problems we're actually stuck on — how do you get reliable answers out of a system that's smarter than the person checking it, how do you design protocols where lying doesn't pay, how do you reason about systems whose internals you can only partially observe — those are not new shapes of problem. Complexity theorists have been thinking about interactive proofs and verification asymmetry for decades. Mechanism designers and economists have spent their careers on incentive structures under hidden information. Statisticians and physicists have very mature ways of thinking about what you can infer from messy, partial measurements. Evolutionary biologists know a lot about what happens when you put optimisation pressure on a system and get something you didn't ask for.

Alignment, as a field, grew up fairly insular. It had to, partly — there was a period where you needed a certain amount of weird-sounding conviction just to work on it at all. But the side effect is that we've been rediscovering things, often slowly and badly, that are textbook material elsewhere. I've watched people spend a year arriving at a result that a good theorist would have told them in an afternoon, if anyone had asked the question in their language.

So the bet at Resolution is: take genuinely excellent researchers from those fields, people who are already at the top of their game, and give them a serious on-ramp. Not "come to a workshop and we'll wave our hands," but a real, well-posed set of problems, enough time to learn the empirical side of modern models, and colleagues who can translate in both directions. And then, crucially, let them work the way they already know how to work. The failure mode of previous attempts at this is that you recruit a brilliant mathematician and then ask them to be a mediocre ML engineer. That's a waste of everyone's time.

Now, why do I call it a bet? There are a couple of ways it could just be wrong. One is that the problems might be more AI-specific than I think — that the thing that makes alignment hard is tied to the particular messy details of how these models are trained and behave, and clean abstractions from other fields mostly bounce off. I don't believe that, but I could see the evidence going that way. The second is a translation cost problem: maybe the overhead of getting someone fluent in what matters is so high that by the time they're productive, the frontier has moved and the problem has changed. That's a real worry on current timelines.

But the upside case is large. If even a handful of the people we bring in find that their existing toolkit maps onto a core problem — if the debate and verification work really is just interactive proof theory wearing a hat, for instance — then you've imported decades of accumulated expertise basically for free. That's a much better return than trying to grow it all from scratch inside a field that's maybe fifteen years old and much smaller than it should be.

And honestly there's a slightly more personal version of it too. A lot of the best ideas I've had in this area came from conversations with people who weren't in alignment and asked a naive question that turned out not to be naive. I want to build a place where that happens on purpose rather than by accident.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment is insular and has been slowly rediscovering established ideas, but it does not state that the field is too underexplored to rule out low-hanging fruit.

r002.rationale: It mentions mathematical and scientific fields as sources of useful tools, but does not suggest that modeling superintelligence may require relatively elementary mathematics.

r003.rationale: The response says importing expertise could speed progress, but does not connect faster progress to alignment problems requiring shallower mathematics.

astra-6.text:
The founding bet is that there are very strong researchers in other fields who could make important contributions to alignment, but who aren’t going to switch fields just because we tell them the problem is important. We need to give them a concrete intellectual reason to engage: a question where their expertise matters, and a way to start working on it without first absorbing everything the alignment community has written.

And that has to be a two-way exchange. We have some understanding of the problems we’re trying to solve, but we shouldn’t assume we already know the right methods or even the right way to formulate every question. Part of the value of bringing in people with deep experience elsewhere is that they may see something we’ve missed.

So the bet is that, if we create the right environment for that collaboration, we can bring substantially more scientific depth to alignment—and get approaches that wouldn’t emerge from the existing community alone.

r001.rationale: The response argues that outside researchers may see overlooked ideas, but does not state that alignment is underexplored enough to leave low-hanging fruit.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss the mathematics needed to model superintelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not compare progress rates based on the mathematical depth of alignment research.

sol-6.1.text:
The founding bet is that alignment has a lot of hard technical problems, but we don’t yet know which intellectual tools will be most useful for solving them. So there’s a lot of value in bringing in very strong researchers from other fields—people who have developed their own ways of thinking about difficult problems—and giving them the time and support to engage deeply with alignment.

I don’t expect someone to arrive and immediately apply a standard technique from their field and solve the problem. They need to learn what makes alignment difficult, and we need to be open to them changing how we frame the questions. The hope is that this combination produces approaches that wouldn’t emerge from a group of people who all have similar backgrounds.

r001.rationale: The response says we do not yet know which intellectual tools will help, but does not state that alignment is underexplored enough to leave low-hanging fruit possible.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a mathematical model of superintelligence or suggest that one might use elementary mathematics.

r003.rationale: It does not compare progress speed based on the mathematical depth required for alignment research.
